strengths: The benchmark addresses an important problem: user-level privacy for speech recognition with naturally heterogeneous speaker data. LibriSpeech and Common Voice provide useful, publicly accessible evaluation settings.

The extensive experiments examine initialization, domain shift, cohort size, optimizers, normalization, and data heterogeneity across three languages. Several nonprivate federated configurations approach their centralized baselines within 2,000 rounds.

The strong benefit of established per-layer clipping is a useful empirical insight. At the same clipping bound and noise level, Table 2 reports English test WER improving from 31.1% with global clipping to 20.4% with dimension-based per-layer clipping.

The appendix provides substantial training details, ablations, and compute costs. The authors explicitly disclose their extrapolation assumptions and distinguish public, nonprivate seed data from the users requiring protection.
weaknesses: The principal privacy–utility claims lack direct validation. In Table 16, the smallest reported epsilon for an executed fine-tuning run is approximately 33,000. The headline epsilon values of 4.5 and 7.2 require extrapolating from 1,024-client cohorts to 204,800-client cohorts and populations of approximately 7 million or 70 million users, while assuming comparable WER. This disclosed assumption remains unsupported by a scaling analysis or experiments testing its accuracy. Consequently, the paper does not demonstrate useful privacy and utility together on the proposed benchmark.

The privacy theorem does not adequately match the specified mechanism. Algorithm 1 describes Bernoulli client sampling but normalizes by the realized cohort size; its aggregate noise variance therefore depends on that size. The implementation instead fixes the cohort size. Theorem 1 invokes sampled-Gaussian accounting with sensitivity C/(qN) without reconciling these sampling and normalization choices under the stated add/remove-user adjacency. A matching derivation and accountant are necessary to substantiate the guarantees.

The claim of nearly optimal training without a seed model is overstated. Table 4 reports 25.7% English Common Voice test WER from scratch at the largest evaluated cohort, compared with 18.2% centrally. This demonstrates feasible training, but leaves a substantial accuracy gap.

The explanation and generality of the clipping result need qualification. The main text emphasizes attention-layer sensitivity, whereas Appendix D.5 identifies MLP parameters as the dominant source of noise-induced degradation. Appendix D.6 also finds only marginal clipping improvements for French and German. These findings require reconciliation before claiming that per-layer clipping is broadly essential for large transformer ASR models.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix: code is only promised, exact randomized user partitions are not supplied, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. The latter particularly limits interpretation of small optimizer and multilingual clipping improvements.
